author: haiku
reason: B is easier for an outsider to get into: it opens with the concrete situation (volumes, the latency need, broker and MailRelay behavior), defines basic terms like ack, SKIP LOCKED and paging on-call, and sets out a short numbered list of rules, with ownership as three states fixed when the notification is enqueued, while A, though it usefully keeps the running system separate from the rollout, buries the reader in claim-time flag logic, NULL-owner edge cases and a much denser text.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier for an outsider to learn from: it opens with what the system does today and why the new design is shaped this way, walks one notification through its runtime path step by step, keeps the rollout in its own section, and adds a failure table. A spreads the same mechanism across invariants and rollout steps, so the reader has to piece together how the system runs.

author: sonnet
reason: A is the one I'd rather be handed. It explains up front how today's system works and why it produces duplicates. It then lays out each component, how ownership passes between the monolith and the service, and what each crash does, with a failure table on top. B covers similar ground but spreads it across longer, repetitive rollout steps, so it is harder to see the whole system.

author: sonnet
reason: B gives a newcomer the clearer picture of how the system works: it first explains today's system and why it duplicates emails (transactional enqueue, 5 s polling, batches of 50, one commit per batch), then describes the finished design as a whole, with rules that always hold, a table of the three email types, the message formats, each part on each side, and a table of what happens when things fail, all before the rollout steps; A spreads its architecture across the rollout steps.

author: haiku
reason: Document A is self-contained for an outsider: it defines every term it relies on, shows the actual table schemas and the exact SQL for creating, checking and sweeping sessions, and explains why things work (for example, capping the idle deadline at the absolute deadline so one condition enforces both); Document B is quicker to read but leaves the `login_failures` schema and the row-lock mechanics for the reader to infer.

author: haiku
reason: B gives an outsider the actual table schema, the exact SQL statements and definitions of stack terms such as transaction, advisory lock and bcrypt, so the system's mechanics are concrete and checkable, while A is tighter but leaves the data model implicit.

author: sonnet
reason: Document A defines the terms an outsider would not know, such as advisory lock, dummy hash and fail closed, and explains the reason for each step and each failure behaviour; it also covers edge cases B leaves out, such as static files and logout skipping the session check, so it is easier to understand without asking anyone.

author: sonnet
reason: B is longer than A but easier for an outsider to follow: it defines the less familiar ideas (advisory lock, dummy hash, middleware, fail closed), gives a reason for each failure behaviour, and covers edge cases A leaves out, such as static files, why logout skips the middleware, and a rollback undoing a counted failure.

author: haiku
reason: A defines the stack terms a newcomer won't know (pod, ReplicaSet, readiness and liveness, rollout, admission rule) and explains why each design choice holds, such as why liveness gets its own path, why old pods stay safe and why revocation comes last, while B is tighter and its key A/B and v1/v2 naming is neat but takes more background knowledge for granted.

author: haiku
reason: B is better for a newcomer because it explains the runtime first and covers how things work today (clients copy keys at import, /healthz reports ok as soon as the listener starts, and the image alone decides which path a pod takes), defines cluster terms such as ReplicaSet, rollback and liveness, and says why each step is safe (for example, the cluster won't stop a rollout of ready pods that the provider rejects), whereas A is tighter but assumes more context.

author: sonnet
reason: A opens with a numbered end-to-end flow and defines the terms an outsider would not know (readiness probe, maxUnavailable: 0, APP_ENV, security on-call). It also says why things happen, such as why old pods keep their keys during the rollout. B is tighter but uses ideas like staging, rolling-deploy mechanics and the canary without explaining them.

author: sonnet
reason: B explains why each step exists and defines the stack terms an outsider lacks, such as the readiness probe, `maxUnavailable: 0`, why old immutable images still hold the old keys, and why the YAML removal and the CI guard must ship in one PR. It also adds a roadmap so the rollout-then-runtime order is easy to follow, while A is tighter but leaves more of the reasoning for the reader to work out.

author: haiku
reason: I'd rather be handed A. It starts with how the system works today and states its assumptions. It defines every term it relies on and explains why each part is built the way it is. It also has a separate sequence diagram for each flow, a token state diagram and a full failure table, so an outsider can follow the mechanism end to end. B is tighter and catches the race with a login in progress, but it gives an outsider less of that context.

author: haiku
reason: B is better for an engineer new to the project: it describes today's system, states up front what the change adds (one table, three endpoints, one page, two emails), explains why each choice was made, and includes a token lifecycle diagram. A is tighter and handles the login race, but its "Keeps X" lines are cryptic and it explains less of the reasoning.

author: sonnet
reason: A explains more of the system on its own terms: it says the reset page is served by the web client and then calls the API (in B, GET /reset appears to go to the API), it describes how sessions, the queue and row locks behave, and it gives the reasons for its choices; B is tighter and its failure table is easier to scan, but it leaves more for an outsider to infer.

author: sonnet
reason: B is denser, but it explains more of what an outsider would otherwise have to guess: what FOR UPDATE does, that the link opens a page on the web client which then calls the API, why the page-load check and the submit check both exist, and that a failed enqueue leaves the user with no working link because the earlier one was already killed.
